title: Insurance Glossary: Plain-English Definitions A to Z
description: Plain-English definitions of insurance terms for home and business cover, from average clause and excess to indemnity period and subrogation.
intro: Insurance has its own language. Here are the terms you’ll meet most often in quotes, policy wordings and claims, in plain English, including the US equivalents.

image.alt: Hand writing notes on white paper at a desk

sections.html: <dl class="gloss"><dt id="policyholder">Policyholder</dt><dd>The person or business that owns the policy.</dd><dt id="premium">Premium</dt><dd>What you pay for the policy, usually yearly or monthly.</dd><dt id="sum-insured">Sum insured</dt><dd>The maximum the insurer will pay for a section of cover, such as buildings or contents.</dd><dt id="limit-of-indemnity">Limit of indemnity</dt><dd>The maximum a liability policy will pay for a claim or in a period.</dd><dt id="policy-wording">Policy wording</dt><dd>The full contract: definitions, cover, exclusions and conditions.</dd><dt id="schedule">Schedule</dt><dd>The page personal to you: who and what is insured, sums insured, excesses and dates.</dd><dt id="ipid">IPID</dt><dd>Insurance Product Information Document: a short standardised summary of a general insurance product (UK and EU).</dd><dt id="endorsement">Endorsement</dt><dd>A change or addition to the standard policy wording, sometimes called a rider in the US.</dd><dt id="peril">Peril</dt><dd>An event that causes loss, such as fire, storm or theft. “Named perils” policies list them; “open perils” policies cover everything not excluded.</dd></dl>

<dl class="gloss"><dt id="excess-deductible">Excess (deductible)</dt><dd>The part of a claim you pay. UK policies have compulsory and voluntary excesses; US policies call it a deductible.</dd><dt id="average-clause">Average clause</dt><dd>A condition that reduces a claim in proportion if you were under-insured.</dd><dt id="new-for-old">New for old</dt><dd>Replacing items with new equivalents rather than paying their second-hand value.</dd><dt id="indemnity">Indemnity</dt><dd>Putting you back in the same financial position as before the loss, no better and no worse.</dd><dt id="insurance-premium-tax-ipt">Insurance Premium Tax (IPT)</dt><dd>UK tax on most general insurance premiums: 12% standard rate, 20% higher rate for some products such as travel insurance.</dd><dt id="premium-finance">Premium finance</dt><dd>Credit used to spread premium payments monthly, which can add interest.</dd><dt id="no-claims-discount">No claims discount</dt><dd>A discount for claim-free years, also called no claims bonus or bonus-malus.</dd></dl>

<dl class="gloss"><dt id="loss-adjuster">Loss adjuster</dt><dd>An expert appointed by the insurer to investigate and value a larger claim.</dd><dt id="loss-assessor">Loss assessor</dt><dd>An expert you can appoint (and pay) to prepare and negotiate your claim.</dd><dt id="subrogation">Subrogation</dt><dd>The insurer’s right, after paying you, to recover the cost from whoever caused the loss.</dd><dt id="contribution">Contribution</dt><dd>Sharing a claim between two insurers when more than one policy covers the same loss.</dd><dt id="settlement">Settlement</dt><dd>The final agreed payment or repair for a claim.</dd><dt id="final-response">Final response</dt><dd>An insurer’s last word on a complaint, after which UK customers can go to the Financial Ombudsman Service.</dd></dl>

<dl class="gloss"><dt id="claims-made">Claims-made</dt><dd>A policy that responds to claims made while it’s in force (typical for PI and D&O).</dd><dt id="occurrence-basis">Occurrence basis</dt><dd>A policy that responds to incidents that happened while it was in force, whenever the claim is made (typical for public liability).</dd><dt id="retroactive-date">Retroactive date</dt><dd>Work done before this date isn’t covered by a claims-made policy.</dd><dt id="run-off-cover">Run-off cover</dt><dd>Protection for claims about past work after a business stops trading.</dd><dt id="indemnity-period">Indemnity period</dt><dd>In business interruption cover, the maximum time the policy pays lost income while you recover.</dd><dt id="gross-profit-insurance">Gross profit (insurance)</dt><dd>Turnover minus specified variable costs; the usual basis for business interruption cover.</dd><dt id="fair-presentation">Fair presentation</dt><dd>A business’s legal duty under the UK Insurance Act 2015 to disclose material facts clearly.</dd><dt id="additional-insured">Additional insured</dt><dd>Another party (such as a client) given protection under your liability policy.</dd></dl>

<dl class="gloss"><dt id="ho-3-ho-5">HO-3 / HO-5</dt><dd>Standard US homeowners policy forms; HO-5 is broader for belongings.</dd><dt id="ho-4-ho-6">HO-4 / HO-6</dt><dd>Renters and condo owner policy forms.</dd><dt id="bop">BOP</dt><dd>Business owner’s policy: property, general liability and business income bundled.</dd><dt id="cgl">CGL</dt><dd>Commercial general liability.</dd><dt id="pip">PIP</dt><dd>Personal injury protection, required in no-fault auto insurance states.</dd><dt id="experience-mod">Experience mod</dt><dd>A multiplier in workers’ comp pricing based on your claims history.</dd><dt id="nfip">NFIP</dt><dd>National Flood Insurance Program, run by FEMA.</dd></dl>
